neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and place. Oriented to month and year but not exact date (1 day off). Mildly disinhibited during exam — makes inappropriate jokes about the examiner's appearance and laughs at her own errors. Utilization behavior observed: picks up the examiner's pen and starts writing on the desk without being asked. MMSE 22/30 — lost 3 points on recall (0/3 words at 5 minutes, retrieved 1 with category cue), lost 1 point on orientation (date), lost 2 points on serial sevens (3 errors), lost 2 points on sentence writing and figure copy (wrote a fragmented sentence, figure copy poorly organized). MoCA 18/30 with deficits in delayed recall (0/5, retrieved 2 with cues), trail-making (0/1), verbal fluency (5 F-words in 60 seconds), clock drawing (2/3 — numbers correct but hand placement imprecise), and abstraction (0/2). Verbal fluency: 8 animals in 60 seconds, 5 F-words in 60 seconds. Applause sign positive — unable to stop clapping at 3 (clapped 7 times). Motor impersistence on tongue protrusion (could not maintain protrusion for 20 seconds).
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial expression mildly flattened. Hearing intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone throughout. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor. No myoclonus. Mild grasp reflexes present bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration sense intact at great toes bilaterally. Proprioception intact. No cortical sensory deficits.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Palmomental reflex present bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base and stride length. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. No gait abnormalities. No postural instability.
neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. Mild bilateral grasp reflexes present. No alien limb phenomenon. Palmomental reflex present bilaterally. Go/no-go task: 4 errors in 10 trials (impaired inhibitory control). Luria hand sequence: could not learn the 3-step sequence after 5 demonstrations (severely impaired).

patient.chief_complaint: Personality changes and poor judgment at work
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sofia Reyes is a 58-year-old right-handed bank branch manager who is referred to the neurology outpatient clinic by her primary care physician for evaluation of progressive behavioral changes and cognitive decline over the past 18 months. Her husband, who accompanies her, provides the majority of the history as the patient tends to minimize and joke about her difficulties. Approximately 18 months ago, her husband first noticed subtle changes in her personality. She began making inappropriate comments to colleagues and customers at the bank, including remarking on a customer's weight and making off-color jokes during staff meetings — behavior completely out of character for someone who had been known for her professionalism and interpersonal skills. Over the following months, she became increasingly apathetic, losing interest in activities she previously enjoyed including running, cooking, and socializing with friends. She has had progressive difficulty with organizational tasks at work — she was previously meticulous with documentation and compliance protocols, but began making errors in loan approvals, forgot to file regulatory reports, and could not manage multiple tasks simultaneously. Her judgment deteriorated — she made several impulsive online purchases totaling over $8,000 in a single month, bought items she already owned, and signed up for multiple streaming subscriptions she never used. After receiving formal complaints from three customers and two staff members about her inappropriate remarks, she was placed on medical leave 4 months ago. She was seen by a psychiatrist who diagnosed depression and tried sertraline 100 mg daily for 8 weeks, then switched to venlafaxine 150 mg for 6 weeks — neither improved her behavioral symptoms, and the language difficulties continued to progress. Importantly, her husband reports that in addition to the behavioral changes, she has developed concurrent memory problems. She frequently forgets conversations from earlier in the day, repeats questions multiple times, forgets appointments despite using calendar reminders, and recently forgot that her daughter had visited the previous weekend. She also has difficulty learning new information — she could not figure out how to use a new coffee maker despite repeated instruction. She has not gotten lost but has had difficulty planning meals and following recipes she previously made from memory. She denies visual hallucinations, paranoid ideation, or delusional thinking. Sleep is unremarkable. There is no history of head trauma, seizures, or substance abuse. Her father's history of behavioral dementia beginning at age 70 is noted.

mri.impression: Frontal-predominant cortical atrophy (bilateral, left greater than right), involving both orbitofrontal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, with mild anterior temporal atrophy. Mild hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens 2) is also present. The frontal-predominant pattern of atrophy, together with the coexisting mild hippocampal atrophy, is atypical for age-related change and suggests a neurodegenerative process; the mixed anterior and medial-temporal distribution is nonspecific and does not point to a single entity. Mild age-appropriate periventricular white matter changes (Fazekas 1). Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly frontal-executive profile. Executive function is severely impaired across multiple measures: Trail Making B discontinued, WCST 1/6 categories completed, Stroop z = −2.4, and Go/No-Go 40% commission errors. Verbal fluency is markedly impaired for both phonemic (FAS 14 total) and semantic (animals 9/min) categories. Episodic memory is also impaired (CVLT-3 long delay 3/16). Clock drawing is mildly impaired (7/10). Visuoconstructive skill and confrontation naming are relatively preserved. Informant behavioral rating (Frontal Behavioral Inventory 32/72) indicates significant behavioral dyscontrol. Profile is consistent with a frontal-executive syndrome with concurrent episodic memory impairment. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Frontal (behavioral/dysexecutive) variant of early-onset Alzheimer's disease

differential.key_features: Clinically the closest mimic — disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, dietary changes; distinguished by amyloid PET (positive in frontal AD, negative in bvFTD) and FDG-PET pattern (temporoparietal hypometabolism in AD vs frontotemporal in FTD)

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder (late-onset mood or personality disorder)
differential.key_features: Behavioral changes at this age can be mistaken for primary psychiatry; objective neuropsychological deficits, progressive course, and biomarker positivity differentiate frontal AD from a psychiatric diagnosis
Lack of motor features (asymmetric rigidity, alien limb, oculomotor abnormalities, postural instability) argues against these atypical parkinsonian syndromes
Excluded by absence of focal vascular lesions on MRI
Excluded by history and review of medications; no exposure to neurotoxic agents or substance use

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed clinical history from patient and informant, including timeline, cognitive domains affected, functional decline, mood, sleep, and medication review
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Gradually progressive cognitive change with informant-confirmed functional impairment in IADLs

optimal_actions.action: Perform bedside cognitive assessment (MMSE and/or MoCA) and detailed neurological examination
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Objective cognitive impairment on MoCA more sensitive than MMSE; non-focal neurological exam (or variant-specific findings — visuospatial in PCA, language in lvPPA, behavioral in frontal AD)

optimal_actions.action: Order reversible-cause labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, folate; consider RPR/HIV per risk)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis) excluded; identify and address co-morbid metabolic factors

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral frontal-predominant cortical atrophy in addition to typical AD-pattern temporoparietal volume loss

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Executive and behavioral dysfunction (impaired set-shifting, poor judgment) often without prominent memory impairment early on

optimal_actions.action: Order CSF biomarkers (Aβ42, Aβ42/40 ratio, p-tau, total tau) for ATN classification
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reduced Aβ42 (or reduced Aβ42/40 ratio) with elevated p-tau supporting A+T+ profile consistent with Alzheimer pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order amyloid PET when CSF biomarkers are unavailable or when diagnostic uncertainty persists after clinical assessment and MRI
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive cortical amyloid retention (SUVr above positivity threshold) confirming amyloid pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order FDG-PET to assess regional metabolism and distinguish AD from frontotemporal dementia or other neurodegenerative patterns
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism that distinguishes frontal AD from bvFTD (which shows frontotemporal hypometabolism)

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No clinically significant interactions; counsel on GI side effects and bradycardia risk

optimal_actions.action: Consider targeted early-onset Alzheimer gene panel (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) if family history suggests autosomal-dominant disease
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pathogenic variant only in a minority of early-onset cases with a strong family history; result informs genetic counseling more than acute management

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis to patient and family, discuss prognosis, advance directives, and driving / safety assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and caregiver engaged in care planning; safety concerns (driving, finances, medication management) addressed

useless_tools.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family
Pursue biomarker confirmation (CSF AT(N) markers or amyloid PET) when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected
Use FDG-PET to characterize the regional metabolic pattern and distinguish atypical AD from FTD or DLB
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
key_reasoning_points: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
Frontal variant AD is the closest mimic of bvFTD; amyloid PET positivity differentiates AD from FTD pathology
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Differentiating frontal variant AD from behavioral variant FTD in a patient with frontal-predominant behavioral and executive deficits, complicated by a family history suggestive of FTD
metadata.educational_value: Teaches recognition of frontal variant AD as an atypical AD presentation that mimics bvFTD, and the critical role of AD biomarkers in differentiating these conditions
key_educational_points: Frontal variant AD can be clinically indistinguishable from bvFTD based on behavioral symptoms alone
Concurrent episodic memory impairment in a behavioral/dysexecutive presentation should raise suspicion for AD rather than pure FTD
AD biomarkers (amyloid PET or CSF) are essential for differentiating frontal AD from bvFTD
FDG-PET showing posterior temporoparietal involvement in addition to frontal hypometabolism favors AD over FTD
Family history of behavioral dementia does not confirm FTD — familial AD can present with frontal symptoms
Negative FTD gene panel (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72) helps exclude genetic FTD but does not rule out sporadic bvFTD
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Behavioral-predominant AD variant that mimics bvFTD; FDG-PET + amyloid PET essential to distinguish (positive amyloid argues against FTD)
